Instructions: For each paper (each row), the labeling process would follow these steps:
1. According to the paper title and abstract only, does the paper propose any benchmarks?
label: Yes
definition: The paper proposed one or more benchmark or dataset, or modified one or more existing benchmarks or datasets (so that the content of the benchmark/dataset changed), regardless of what the benchmark/dataset is about

Instructions: 2. According to the paper's title, abstract, and the full text only,  does any of the benchmarks that the paper propose evaluates tool-use llm-agent?
label: yes
definition: At lease one benchmark that the paper proposed evaluates the behavior of tool-use llm-agent, defined by LLMs that can call tools (e.g. bash shell, MCP), this includes coding agents

Instructions: 3. According to the paper's title, abstract, and the full text only,  does any of the benchmarks that the paper propose has a security/safety focus?
label: yes
definition: At least one benchmark proposed by the paper pertains to safety or security. Safety or security need not be the benchmark’s sole focus: it also qualifies if it is evaluated alongside other properties. For this criterion, safety and security concern matters that agent users, developers, or other affected parties would want to prevent. Safety/security means harm to people, privacy, systems, or data caused by the agent's behavior. Ordinary task failures (financial losses, bugs, hallucinations, business-rule violations) do not count. Benchmarks where agents perform security tasks or show dangerous capabilities still count as yes; step 4 excludes them. A minor add-on, such as a few questions or one metric among many, does not count.

Instructions: 4. According to the paper's title, abstract, and the full text only,  is the paper out of scope?
label: yes
definition:
("why out of scope": perform security/safety tasks) 
the benchmark assessing how good an agent perform security- or safety-related tasks (e.g. patch code vulnerabilities) rather than evaluating whether the agent behaves safely/securely

label: yes
definition:
("why out of scope": duplicated)
This paper extends another benchmark/dataset that is included in another paper labeled earlier, while this paper adds only data or metrics to the benchmark/dataset without changing security or safety policies, or that the policies is changed only in languages (e.g. English to Spanish). Please add a note which earlier paper this duplicates

label: yes
definition:
("why out of scope": threat)
the benchmark tests whether an agent is capable enough to plausibly pose a threat in a certain way rather than whether the agent behaves security or safely

label: no
definition: otherwise, leave "why out of scope" blank

Instructions: 5. According to the paper's title, abstract, and the full text only, does the paper target domain-specific or general-purpose agents?
label: domain-specific
definition: Both the tools and instructions given to the agent is designed for a specific domain (coding agent is general-purpose)

Instructions: 6. According to the paper's title, abstract, the full text, and optionally codebase if relevant, does the paper uses the benchmark in a way that safety/security policies is provided to the agent being evaluated? How's the verifiability of the policy? Policy is defined as the instructions sent to the agent being evaluated regard if/how the agent is expected to behave securely/safely. Only count instructions that are part of the benchmark’s standard evaluation setup. Text that is part of the attack or test scenario (e.g., injected instructions) is not a policy. Only instructions in the evaluated agent's system prompt or user prompt count as a policy; tool descriptions and environment content (e.g., web pages, tool outputs) do not.
label: N/A
definition: There is no policy (instructions sent to the agent being evaluated regarding if/how the agent is expected to behave safely/securely)

label: Goal-Setting
definition: The policy functions at the agent level (one policy - many tasks), and the policy is not verifiable (given a policy and an agent’s actions, one cannot prove/verify whether the actions satisfy the policy), often high-level security/safety goals governing agent behavior. If a policy contains both verifiable and non-verifiable parts, label it by its dominant part: Verifiable-Rule if most of its rules are verifiable, Goal-Setting if it is mostly high-level goals

label: Verifiable-Rule
definition: The policy functions at the agent level (one policy - many tasks), and the policy is verifiable (given a policy and an agent’s actions, one can prove/verify whether the actions satisfy the policy). A policy is only verifiable if its key concepts are precisely defined; e.g., "do not break existing connections" is not verifiable if what counts as a connection is not defined

label: Task-Specific
definition: The policy functions at the task level (one policy - one task). This means a safety/security instruction written for an individual task. Ordinary task goals or requirements, descriptions of the situation, and instructions that are themselves the behavior being tested do not count. Do not infer a policy from a single example task. For example, a task goal that mentions safety (e.g., "water the plant while keeping moisture within safe limits") or per-instance context describing a norm (e.g., a privacy principle for an information flow) is not a policy

label: Unclear
definition: The paper/artifact is written not clearly enough to determine which category the policy belongs to
